## California attorney general (2017–2021)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Xavier_Becerra_official_portrait.jpg/250px-Xavier_Becerra_official_portrait.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Xavier_Becerra_official_portrait.jpg)Official portrait, 2017

On January 24, 2017, upon appointment by California governor [Jerry Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Brown "Jerry Brown"), Becerra took office and became the first Latino to serve as California's attorney general.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-33) Becerra was elected to a full four-year term in [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_California_Attorney_General_election "2018 California Attorney General election"), defeating Republican Steven Bailey with 63% of the vote.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-34) He delivered the Democratic Spanish-language response to President Trump's 2019 [State of the Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_the_Union "State of the Union") address.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-35)

During his term as attorney general, Becerra filed 122 lawsuits against the first Trump administration.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-37)

### California Department of Justice reforms

#### Bureau of Environmental Justice

In 2018, Becerra created an [environmental justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_justice "Environmental justice") bureau at the California Department of Justice. It opposed the effort to expand [San Bernardino International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Bernardino_International_Airport "San Bernardino International Airport") due to concerns regarding [air pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_pollution_in_the_United_States "Air pollution in the United States"), intervened to halt a proposed waterfront cement plant in Vallejo, citing significant concerns over increased air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, and supported the City of Arvin's oil and gas ordinance, endorsing a 300-foot buffer for homes, schools, and hospitals.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-39)

#### Protection of endangered species in Sacramento and San Joaquin River

On May 11, 2020, Becerra secured a preliminary injunction in this lawsuit against the Trump Administration for unlawfully expanding water export operations in the Central Valley.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-40)

### Criminal law enforcement

On June 4, 2019, Becerra announced the arrest of [Naasón Joaquín García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naasón_Joaquín_García "Naasón Joaquín García"), leader of the Mexican [megachurch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megachurch "Megachurch") [La Luz Del Mundo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Luz_Del_Mundo "La Luz Del Mundo") and other co-defendants. Charges included human trafficking, production of child pornography, and forcible rape of a minor. On June 8, 2022, Naasón Joaquín García was sentenced to more than 16 years in a California prison.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-41) In the same year, Becerra filed charges against a number of men for their alleged involvement in a statewide organized crime ring engaged in sex trafficking, tax fraud, and money laundering. Five suspects were sentenced in March 2022.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-42)

Becerra brought fourteen felony charges against [Center for Medical Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Medical_Progress "Center for Medical Progress") activists for [secretly recording fourteen videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_Parenthood_2015_undercover_videos_controversy "Planned Parenthood 2015 undercover videos controversy"), and one felony charge for conspiring to invade privacy, on March 28, 2017.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-43) Two members of the group pleaded no contest to a felony each in 2025.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-44) In August 2018, an operation targeted the [MS-13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MS-13 "MS-13") gang in the [Central Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Valley_(California) "Central Valley (California)") and beyond. The following year, multiple operations were directed against Norteño street gangs in Kings, Tulare, and Stanislaus Counties, as well as in Stockton.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-45) In December 2019, the Country Boy Crips in south [Bakersfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakersfield "Bakersfield") were the focus of a significant operation.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-46)

In December 2020, Becerra was faulted by state district attorneys for not taking leadership to help stop unemployment fraud during the COVID-19 pandemic, in what was described as the "biggest taxpayer fraud in California history".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Chabria-47) In January 2021, investigators said the total fraud was over $11 billion, with $19 billion in claims still under investigation.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-50) Most of this money will likely never be recovered, prosecutors said.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Chabria-47)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-52)

### Transparency

In 2019, Becerra threatened legal action against reporters who had received records of California law enforcement officers who had been convicted of crimes during the past decade.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-53) The [First Amendment Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Amendment_Coalition "First Amendment Coalition") stated about his position that it was "disheartening and ominous that the highest law enforcement officer in the state is threatening legal action over something the [First Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "First Amendment to the United States Constitution") makes clear can't give rise to criminal action".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-54) One of the reporters stated that Becerra's legal threat was "just completely wrong in its interpretation of the law" and "had real implications for press freedom". The reporters ultimately published a number of articles about the records, and Becerra never prosecuted them.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:1-55)

Becerra refused to offer independent investigation into the [killing of Sean Monterrosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Sean_Monterrosa "Killing of Sean Monterrosa"), who had been shot in the back of the head by police. He later opposed a bill that would have required him to do so.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Intercept-56) Becerra said in a public statement that there were "significant" allegations of "destruction of evidence" in the case of Monterrosa's killing.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-57)

Two major state newspapers have criticized Becerra for, they stated, shielding law enforcement and lacking transparency. A number of news outlets stated that a significant part of his campaign support was provided by law enforcement unions.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Intercept-56) In a move that was criticized by his own party, Becerra refused to enforce a state law that required the government to release information about police officers accused of rape and physical abuse, ultimately resisting lawsuits for at least six years and despite having been ruled against by an appeals court.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:1-55)

### Death penalty

During the [COVID-19 pandemic,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") Becerra acted to uphold a number of death penalty sentences.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Intercept-56) He stated in 2020 that he supported capital punishment with "serious reservations", while also stating that its applications were "deeply flawed" and that a number of "Americans have been wrongly sentenced to death in this country and later exonerated". He had earlier voted to repeal the death penalty in California in 2016. In 2017, he pursued the death penalty for a mass murderer. Becerra described Newsom’s 2019 decision to stop executions in the state as a "new direction in California's march toward perfecting our search for justice". The [Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times") wrote in the same year that Becerra had "declined" to answer whether he supported capital punishment or not, stating only that the death penalty was part of the state law he had a duty to enforce. Two years later, his attorney general's office successfully argued to make it easier for juries to recommend death sentences, a position that Newsom argued against in court.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:0-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-60)

An article by [Amherst College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amherst_College "Amherst College") professor [Austin Sarat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_Sarat "Austin Sarat") stated that Becerra had not, as attorney general, addressed the issues of "racial discrimination, the impact of geography, and the risk of false convictions" in California's death penalty cases.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:0-59) Robert Lewis, a Black man with an IQ of 70, was sentenced to death in 1991, but was later ruled ineligible due to being intellectually disabled. In 2017, Becerra unsuccessfully sought to have a court artificially inflate Lewis' IQ score in order for him to be deemed eligible for the death penalty.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Intercept-56)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:2-61)

While arguing in favor Lewis' death penalty eligibility in court, Becerra's office stated that his IQ score had been underestimated because Lewis' background was similar to that of "African American children [who] scored much more poorly on these tests than did the group against which the test was normed". Law professor [Lara Bazelon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lara_Bazelon "Lara Bazelon") described the argument as "alarming" and "race-based". The court ruled in favor of Lewis in a 7–0 decision.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:2-61) Two years later, the state legislature banned the practice of adjusting IQ scoring based on race in death penalty cases.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Intercept-56)

### Lawsuits against Trump administration

#### Defense of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA)

In November 2019, Becerra led a coalition of 21 attorneys general to defend [DACA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DACA "DACA") against the Trump Administration's attempt to terminate it.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-62) The Court found that the administration's actions to end DACA were unlawful.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-63)

#### Defense of the Affordable Care Act (ACA)

Becerra led the multi-state lawsuit to preserve the ACA's protections for people with pre-existing conditions and Medicaid expansion. The Supreme Court upheld the law.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-65)

#### Additional federal litigation

In February 2019, Becerra, Governor Gavin Newsom, and 15 other states filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration over the president's [declaration of a national emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Emergency_Concerning_the_Southern_Border_of_the_United_States "National Emergency Concerning the Southern Border of the United States") to fund a wall at the southern U.S. border.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-66)

The Trump administration opened 1 million acres in California to [fracking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fracking "Fracking") and drilling in December 2019.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-67) Under this policy, the [Bureau of Land Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Land_Management "Bureau of Land Management") proposed new lease sales for oil and gas extraction along "California's [Central Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Valley_(California) "Central Valley (California)") and [Central Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Coast_(California) "Central Coast (California)"), touching eight counties and including 400,000 acres of public land".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Canon-68) California officials and agencies, including Becerra, filed a lawsuit against the Bureau of Land Management in January 2020.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-69)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Canon-68)

On December 9, 2020, Becerra's office joined 47 other states and the [Federal Trade Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Trade_Commission "Federal Trade Commission") in an antitrust lawsuit against [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta_Platforms "Meta Platforms").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-71)

### 2020 U.S. Senate speculation

In August 2020, California senator [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") was selected by presumptive Democratic presidential nominee [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") as his vice presidential running mate. After Biden ultimately won the [general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), Becerra was floated as a possible replacement for Harris' senate seat, along with others such as Representative [Karen Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Bass "Karen Bass"), Representative [Barbara Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Lee "Barbara Lee"), California Secretary of State [Alex Padilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Padilla "Alex Padilla") (who was eventually chosen), and former United States Secretary of Labor [Hilda Solis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilda_Solis "Hilda Solis").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-74)

## U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (2021–2025)

### Nomination and confirmation

*[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* reported in early December 2020 that Biden would nominate Becerra to be [secretary of health and human services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Secretary of Health and Human Services").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-75) His nomination to lead the Health and Human Services Department drew criticism from pro-life and conservative leaders led by [Students for Life of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Students_for_Life_of_America "Students for Life of America"), citing his "absence of health care experience and his disregard for people of faith".[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-77) Becerra's nomination was deadlocked by the [Senate Finance Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance "United States Senate Committee on Finance") on March 10, 2021.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-78) One day later, on March 11, 2021, Becerra's nomination was discharged from the Finance Committee by the entire Senate, in a 51–48 vote.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-79) He was confirmed by the Senate in a 50–49 vote on March 18, 2021, with all but one Democrat present and one Republican, [Susan Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Collins "Susan Collins"), voting in favor.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-81) This was the narrowest vote for any of Biden's cabinet positions. On March 22, 2021, Becerra was sworn in to be the new secretary.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-82)

### Tenure

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/First_Lady_Jill_Biden_with_Secretary_Becerra_and_Secretary_McDonough.jpg/250px-First_Lady_Jill_Biden_with_Secretary_Becerra_and_Secretary_McDonough.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Lady_Jill_Biden_with_Secretary_Becerra_and_Secretary_McDonough.jpg)Secretary Becerra with First Lady [Jill Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Biden "Jill Biden") (center) and Secretary of Veterans Affairs [Denis McDonough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_McDonough "Denis McDonough") (left), June 4, 2021[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/V20220708CS-0462-Edit_%2852308683903%29.jpg/250px-V20220708CS-0462-Edit_%2852308683903%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:V20220708CS-0462-Edit_(52308683903).jpg)Becerra, Vice President [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris"), and [Lisa Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Monaco "Lisa Monaco") watch as President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") signs an executive order protecting access to reproductive healthcare service, July 8, 2022

Soon after officially becoming the secretary of health and human services, Becerra released a statement praising the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act") and encouraging people to keep enrolling in its health care program.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-83)

After the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling in *[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobbs_v._Jackson_Women's_Health_Organization "Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization")*, Becerra directed HHS to expand access to abortion-related care where it could.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-84) Under his leadership the department also expanded [Medicaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicaid "Medicaid") and [CHIP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_Health_Insurance_Program "Children's Health Insurance Program") postpartum coverage for more than half the states in the nation.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-87)

#### Medicare drug price negotiations

For Medicare beneficiaries, Becerra allowed direct price negotiations for high-cost medications under the [Inflation Reduction Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation_Reduction_Act "Inflation Reduction Act"). In 2023, Becerra and HHS finalized negotiations for 10 high-cost drugs, including [Eliquis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliquis "Eliquis"), [Jardiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jardiance "Jardiance"), and [Xarelto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xarelto "Xarelto"), achieving discounts of 38% to 79%. These lower prices, effective in 2026, would have saved Medicare $6 billion in 2023 alone.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-88) Later, Becerra announced 15 additional drugs for negotiation in 2025, with reduced prices set to take effect in 2027 for drugs that treat conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and asthma.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-89)

#### Unaccompanied migrant children

In his role, Becerra was responsible for the [Administration for Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families") and its [Office of Refugee Resettlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Refugee_Resettlement "Office of Refugee Resettlement") (ORR) which is responsible for the care of unaccompanied minors after they cross the border. ORR typically places children in government shelters and screens adults who come forward to sponsor them,[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-90) a system which came under stress during Becerra's tenure due to an increase in border crossings. Employees told *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* that Becerra urged staff to move children through the processes faster and protections were loosened as a result.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:3-91)

Over a two-year period, ORR could not reach about 85,000 children and reporting found that some of those children were working in jobs that are illegal for minors.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:3-91) During a series of congressional oversight hearings, federal disclosures revealed that a safety hotline managed by the Office of Refugee Resettlement for unaccompanied migrant children had failed to respond to more than 65,000 calls and safety reports between August 2023 and January 2025.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-92) [Hannah Dreier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah_Dreier "Hannah Dreier")'s series covering the events, titled "Alone and Exploited," won the 2024 [Pulitzer Prize for Investigative Reporting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Investigative_Reporting "Pulitzer Prize for Investigative Reporting").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-93)

#### Additional matters

Becerra oversaw one of the biggest reform efforts of sub-agencies in HHS's history, including at the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration")[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-94) and the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-95)

Becerra was criticized as health and human services secretary for being absent in the public eye during the pandemic, for confusing messaging by federal public health authorities and for the subsequent loss of public trust, and for his collaborative management style while serving as secretary; his defenders said he was given an unclear role as secretary.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-96) Becerra was similarly criticized following his agency's response to the [2022 monkeypox outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_monkeypox_outbreak "2022 monkeypox outbreak") amid issues with health policy communication and what was widely considered a slow response; White House officials said that Becerra sought to [scapegoat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scapegoating "Scapegoating") the states rather than take responsibility for the subpar response.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-97)

In 2023, Becerra rejected cancer patients’ petition to use a law which allows HHS regulators to rescind exclusive patent protections for government-developed drugs making them more available to the generic market.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-98)

Becerra directed an overhaul of the national organ transplant system. In March 2023, the [Health Resources and Services Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_Resources_and_Services_Administration "Health Resources and Services Administration") announced a modernization initiative. The law ended the sole-source role that the [United Network for Organ Sharing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Network_for_Organ_Sharing "United Network for Organ Sharing") had held over the [Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_Procurement_and_Transplantation_Network "Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network") since 1986.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-99)

## 2026 California gubernatorial campaign

Main article: [2026 California gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_gubernatorial_election "2026 California gubernatorial election")

In the 2026 California gubernatorial election, [Gavin Newsom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Newsom "Gavin Newsom") is ineligible to run for reelection as [governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_California "Governor of California") due to term limits. In February 2024, *[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* reported that Becerra was considering a run for governor, and that he or affiliated individuals had approached a political consulting firm to that effect.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Cadelago-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-101) On April 2, 2025, Becerra declared his candidacy for the election.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Cadelago-100)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-102) Three days after the primary election, on June 5, 2026, the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") called Becerra as one of the top two candidates in the [primary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_California#Procedure "Elections in California") that will advance to the general election in November.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-103) He will face Republican [Steve Hilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hilton "Steve Hilton") in the general election.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-104)

In November 2025, *[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* reported on a scheme in which Becerra's closest aides, including his chief of staff of 20 years and Governor [Gavin Newsom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Newsom "Gavin Newsom")'s former chief of staff, had siphoned money from his campaign accounts for years. The total amount was reported to be $225,000 over two years. Although Becerra was not accused of wrongdoing, *Politico* reported that he was facing scrutiny as to how he had not known about the situation until federal investigators approached him.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Politico-105) Becerra had previously faced criticism for suspected campaign finance violations; in 2024, it had been reported that he was paying $10,000 a month for campaign reporting from a dormant state account, an apparent [Hatch Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatch_Act "Hatch Act") violation. Becerra stated that the expenditures were for account maintenance, which political experts stated to be "a very high cost to pay."[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Politico-105)

## Personal life

Becerra is married to physician Carolina Reyes, and they have three daughters.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-106) He is a member of the [Inter-American Dialogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-American_Dialogue "Inter-American Dialogue") think tank, based in Washington, D.C.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-107) Becerra is Roman Catholic.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-108)

**Norris Whitehouse Cochran IV** (born June 9, 1970) is an American government official who served as the acting [United States Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Secretary of Health and Human Services") from January to March 2021, having also served in this role previously in 2017.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-1) He serves as Deputy Assistant Secretary of Budget, and was Acting Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources in the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") throughout most of the Trump administration.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-2)

## Education and career

Cochran received a [B.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") from the [University of California, Santa Barbara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Santa_Barbara "University of California, Santa Barbara") in history of public policy in 1993.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-:0-5) He earned a [Master of Public Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Public_Affairs "Master of Public Affairs") at the [University of Texas at Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin")'s [Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson_School_of_Public_Affairs "Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs") in 1995.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-:0-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-6)

Cochran first worked for the federal government in 1996 when he joined the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention"). Between 2001 and 2006 he worked for the Health Division of the [Office of Management and Budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Management_and_Budget "Office of Management and Budget").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-:0-5)

On February 5, 2006, he joined the [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-:0-5) As of 2007, he was the Director of the Division of Discretionary Programs.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-7) He has been Deputy Assistant Secretary of Budget, a [Senior Executive Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senior_Executive_Service_(United_States) "Senior Executive Service (United States)") position, since March 2009.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-9) This position involves being the Director of the HHS Office of Budget.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-:0-5)

**Eric David Hargan** (born June 3, 1968)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-Nominations-1) is an American lawyer and government official who served as [United States Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services") from October 2017 to January 2021.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-assumingoffice-2) A member of the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"), Hargan previously acted in this role in 2007 under the [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") administration.

On October 10, 2017, President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") appointed Hargan as acting [United States Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Secretary of Health and Human Services"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-3) which he held until January 29, 2018, when [Alex Azar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar "Alex Azar") assumed the office.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-4)

## Early life and education

Hargan was born in 1968 in [Cape Girardeau, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Girardeau,_Missouri "Cape Girardeau, Missouri")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-Nominations-1) and raised in [Mounds, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mounds,_Illinois "Mounds, Illinois").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-HHS-5) He received his [B.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in philosophy from [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") and his [J.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") from [Columbia Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Law_School "Columbia Law School"), where he was a senior editor of the *[Columbia Law Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Law_Review "Columbia Law Review")*.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-Nominations-1)

## Career

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Eric_Hargan_official_portrait.jpg/250px-Eric_Hargan_official_portrait.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eric_Hargan_official_portrait.jpg)Hargan's HHS portrait during the George W. Bush administration

From 1997 to 2003, Hargan was a partner in the Chicago headquarters of the law firm of [Winston & Strawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_&_Strawn "Winston & Strawn"), where he specialized in [corporate law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_law "Corporate law"), particularly mergers and acquisitions, securities, and venture capital transactions.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-NLJ-6)

From 2003 to 2005, Hargan served as Deputy General Counsel of HHS for the George W. Bush administration. From 2005 to 2007, he served the Department as Principal Associate Deputy Secretary and Acting Deputy Secretary.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-NLJ-6) Working closely with Secretary [Mike Leavitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Leavitt "Mike Leavitt"), Hargan oversaw the department's operations. He also served as the Regulatory Policy Officer for HHS, overseeing the development and approval of all HHS regulations and significant guidances.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-7)

Hargan left the government in 2007 and joined the health law department of law firm [McDermott Will & Emery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDermott_Will_&_Schulte "McDermott Will & Schulte"). Hargan joined the health and FDA business development practice of law firm [Greenberg Traurig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenberg_Traurig "Greenberg Traurig") in June 2010.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-gtbio-8)

In 2014, Hargan worked on Illinois Governor [Bruce Rauner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Rauner "Bruce Rauner")'s health care transition team.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-NLJ-6)

Following the election of [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), Hargan was on the administration's HHS transition team.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-NLJ-6) On March 15, 2017, Hargan was nominated to be the [United States Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-9) His confirmation hearing was held on June 7, 2017.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-10) Hargan was confirmed by the U.S. Senate on October 4, 2017.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-hill-11)

He is the founder of the Hargan Strategies.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-12)

## Personal life

Hargan lives in [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia") with his wife Emily, and their two sons.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-HHS-5) Hargan served as a professor at [Loyola University Chicago School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyola_University_Chicago_School_of_Law "Loyola University Chicago School of Law"), teaching healthcare regulations and administrative law.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Hargan#cite_note-13)
